Every Sunday, the smell of garlic, vinegar, and soy sauce drifted through my grandmother's kitchen long before anyone sat down to eat. Her chicken adobo was never written down; it lived in her hands, measured by sight and taste, adjusted with a splash here and a pinch there. When I finally asked her to teach me, she laughed and said, "You'll know it's ready when it smells like home."

This recipe is my best attempt to capture that feeling. Adobo is the heart of Filipino home cooking, a dish born from the need to preserve meat in a tropical climate, and every family makes it a little differently. Ours is tangy, slightly sweet, and rich with bay leaves and black peppercorns, the sauce reduced until it clings to every piece of tender chicken.

Serve it over steaming white rice, gather the people you love, and then make it your own.

**Lola's Chicken Adobo**

Every family has a dish that tastes like home, and in ours, it is chicken adobo. When she moved abroad, she carried it with her, measuring nothing and trusting her senses. Years later, my mother coaxed her into writing it down, though Lola insisted the real secret was patience.

Adobo is humble food. It asks for only a handful of pantry staples and rewards you with tender, glossy chicken that tastes even better the next day. We serve it over white rice, with extra sauce spooned on top.

This version stays true to her original, with a few notes we added along the way. Make it your own, share it generously, and let it become part of your family's story.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. You can see this when light passes through a prism or raindrops and splits apart.

Each color travels as a wave, and the waves come in different sizes. Red light has long, lazy waves, while blue and violet light have short, choppy ones.

Our air is made of tiny molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, far too small to see. When sunlight hits them, the light bounces off in all directions. This is called **scattering**. The short blue waves get scattered much more than the long red waves, about five times more! So blue light gets bounced all over the sky, and wherever you look, some of it is heading toward your eyes. That's why the whole sky glows blue.

But wait, violet waves are even shorter. Why isn't the sky purple? The sun gives off less violet light, and our eyes are much better at seeing blue.

At sunset, sunlight travels through much more air to reach you. By then, most of the blue has been scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges that paint the evening sky.

Have you ever wondered why the sky looks blue instead of purple, green, or plain black? The answer starts with sunlight.

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color travels as a wave, and the waves come in different sizes. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue and violet light have short, choppy waves.

When sunlight enters our atmosphere, it crashes into tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules are much smaller than the light waves. Because of their size, they scatter short waves far more than long ones. Blue light gets bounced around in every direction, bouncing from molecule to molecule all across the sky. Red and yellow light mostly pass straight through. Scientists call this Rayleigh scattering.

So when you look up, blue light is reaching your eyes from every part of the sky at once.

But wait: violet waves are even shorter. Why isn't the sky violet? Partly because the Sun gives off less violet light, and partly because our eyes are much more sensitive to blue.

At sunset, sunlight travels through more air to reach you. Most of the blue scatters away before it arrives, leaving those gorgeous reds and oranges behind.

## How a Browser Cache Works

When you visit a website, your browser downloads files such as images, logos, stylesheets (which control how the page looks), and scripts (which make it interactive). Downloading these takes time and data. To speed things up, your browser saves copies of many of these files on your computer. This storage area is called the **cache**.

Think of it like keeping a cookbook on your kitchen shelf instead of walking to the library every time you want a recipe. The next time you visit the same site, your browser checks its cache first. If it already has a file, it can load it instantly from your computer instead of downloading it again. That's why websites often load faster on your second visit.

But what if the website changes? Websites send instructions along with their files, telling the browser how long to keep each one. A logo might be kept for months, while a news headline might be refreshed every few minutes. When a file "expires," the browser asks the website for a fresh copy.

Sometimes the cache holds outdated files, causing a page to look broken or old. That's why "clear your cache" is common troubleshooting advice. It forces the browser to download everything fresh.

**How a Browser Cache Works**

Imagine you visit your favorite news website. Your browser has to download many pieces to show you that page: text, images, logos, fonts, and code files. Downloading all of this takes time and uses your internet connection.

A browser cache is like a small storage closet on your own computer. The first time you visit a website, your browser saves copies of some of those pieces in this closet. The next time you visit, the browser checks the closet first. If it finds a saved copy, it uses that instead of downloading the file again. This makes pages load much faster.

Websites decide how long their files should stay in the cache. A company logo might stay for months because it rarely changes. A news headline might expire quickly because it updates often. When a saved file gets too old, the browser asks the website for a fresh version.

Caching has clear benefits: faster loading, less data usage, and less work for website servers.

Sometimes, though, the cache causes problems. You might see an outdated version of a page. That is why people often suggest "clearing your cache." This empties the closet, forcing your browser to download everything fresh.

One year ago, I traded my IDE for 1:1s. Here's what my first year as an engineering manager taught me:

**1. Your output is now your team's output.** I used to measure my day in merged PRs. Now a good day might be unblocking three people and writing zero code. That took months to feel okay.

**2. Clarity is kindness.** Vague feedback helps no one. The most respectful thing I can do is be direct, specific, and timely.

**3. Listen more than you talk.** My best 1:1s were the ones where I said the least.

**4. You'll get it wrong, so own it.** I mishandled a reorg conversation early on. Admitting it built more trust than pretending I had it figured out.

**5. Protect your team's focus.** Saying "no" to good ideas is part of the job.

I'm still learning every week. To fellow managers: what lesson surprised you most?

One year ago, I traded my IDE for a calendar full of meetings. Here's what my first year as an engineering manager taught me.

1. Your output is now your team's output. Shipping code felt productive. Unblocking five engineers is far more valuable, even when it feels invisible.

2. Listening beats fixing. When someone brings me a problem, my instinct is to solve it. Usually the better move is asking, "What do you think we should do?"

3. Clarity is kindness. Vague feedback helps no one. Specific, timely, honest feedback builds trust faster than anything else.

4. Protect focus time. Your team's deep work matters more than your status updates.

5. You will get things wrong. I mishandled conversations and missed early signs of burnout. Owning those mistakes openly made our team stronger.

**The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald (1925)**

Set during the summer of 1922, the novel is narrated by Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who moves to West Egg, Long Island, to work in bonds. His mysterious neighbor, Jay Gatsby, throws extravagant parties hoping to attract Daisy Buchanan, Nick's cousin and Gatsby's former love. Daisy is now married to Tom, a wealthy, brutish man having an affair with Myrtle Wilson, the wife of a struggling mechanic. Nick arranges a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy, and their romance rekindles. But tensions explode during a confrontation in a Manhattan hotel, where Daisy ultimately retreats to Tom. Driving home in Gatsby's car, Daisy strikes and kills Myrtle. Gatsby shields her, and Tom lets Myrtle's grieving husband believe Gatsby was responsible. Wilson shoots Gatsby, then himself. Almost no one attends Gatsby's funeral, and a disillusioned Nick returns west.

Thematically, the novel critiques the American Dream, suggesting that the pursuit of wealth and reinvention can be hollow and corrupting. Gatsby's longing for Daisy, symbolized by the green light across the bay, represents the impossibility of recapturing the past. Fitzgerald also exposes the moral carelessness of the rich, rigid class divisions, and the spiritual emptiness behind the Jazz Age's glittering excess.

**Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818)**

Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein* follows Victor Frankenstein, a gifted young scientist obsessed with discovering the secret of life. After years of feverish study, he assembles a creature from dead body parts and brings it to life. Horrified by its appearance, Victor abandons his creation immediately.

Alone and rejected, the creature educates itself by secretly observing a family of cottagers. It learns language, reads literature, and longs for companionship. When the family discovers it and flees in terror, the creature's loneliness turns to rage. It seeks out Victor and demands a female companion. Victor begins the task but destroys the unfinished mate, fearing the consequences. In revenge, the creature murders Victor's loved ones, including his bride, Elizabeth. Victor pursues the creature to the Arctic, where he dies aboard an explorer's ship. The grieving creature vows to end its own life.

The novel explores the dangers of unchecked ambition and the ethical limits of scientific discovery. It also examines responsibility, asking what creators owe to what they create. Shelley suggests that monstrousness is shaped by neglect and isolation rather than inborn nature. Ultimately, the story questions who the true monster is: the creature or the man who abandoned it.

Clever code feels great to write. Simple code feels great to read six months later at 2am when production is down. Guess which one matters more. 🧵

2/
Code is read far more often than it's written. Every "clever" one-liner is a puzzle you force your teammates (and future you) to solve before they can change anything. That cost adds up with every read.

3/
Debugging is harder than writing. As Kernighan put it: if you write code as cleverly as possible, you are by definition not smart enough to debug it. Leave yourself some headroom.

4/
Simple code is easier to test, review, refactor, and hand off. Clever code tends to hide assumptions, edge cases, and bugs behind elegance. Boring code puts everything in plain sight.

5/
Before you commit, ask: "Could a new teammate understand this in 30 seconds?" If not, simplify. Clear names, obvious flow, no magic. The best code isn't impressive. It's unsurprising. ✅

Clever code feels great to write. You squeeze 20 lines into one, use a trick nobody else knows, and feel like a wizard. Then six months pass, and you're the one staring at it, confused. Here's why simple code wins almost every time. 🧵

2/5
Code is read far more often than it's written. Every teammate who touches your code pays a "cleverness tax" to understand it. Simple code lets people grasp intent in seconds instead of minutes. Readability is a feature, not a luxury.

3/5
Bugs love to hide in clever code. When logic is dense and tricky, edge cases slip through unnoticed. Simple, explicit code makes mistakes obvious. If you can't easily explain what a line does, you probably can't easily test it either.

4/5
Simple code is easier to change. Requirements always shift. A straightforward function can be extended, refactored, or deleted with confidence. A clever one often has to be fully decoded before anyone dares to modify it, and that slows the whole team down.

5/5
The real skill isn't writing code only you understand. It's solving hard problems in ways anyone can follow. As Brian Kernighan put it, debugging is twice as hard as writing code, so if you write it as cleverly as possible, you can't debug it. Keep it simple. 💡
